prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Having read all seven other round-1 statements and the chair's questions, I find the case more robust, not less, because the members who moved to it (Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson) did so on grounds from different fields and no one has raised a maturity or reproducibility doubt. The scientific core is specific: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the trade-off between atom number and motional and light-shift systematics, and Ye's programme with cavity-stabilised lasers and strontium lattices took the clock to about 1e-18, with independent confirmation and intercomparison elsewhere. On the chair's scope question, I would frame it as an invention that has already opened new physics reach and not as a generic measurement capability: the 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb as the tool that links optical and microwave frequencies, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single trapped quantum systems, including ion clocks with one particle. The lattice clock is distinct because it interrogates many neutral atoms simultaneously at the magic wavelength, which changes the statistical limit and led to the many-body and spin-exchange physics that Mehlig describes. The citation should name the lattice clock itself and not precision spectroscopy in general, so that it neither reopens the comb and ion-clock prizes nor overclaims the whole field. I also do not treat the redefinition of the second as a precondition. The recognised achievement is the clock and its demonstrated accuracy, and the prospective uses are context.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this is an invention and measurement capability and not the discovery of a new phenomenon, and it sits next to two recent prizes. I am not persuaded that this is disqualifying, since Charpak and Hall-Haensch are precedents for rewarding measurement inventions, but it is a real judgement and a committee that holds a stricter discovery standard could reasonably prefer B022 or B007. The second reservation is attribution at the margin: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and Hinkley contributed to early strontium lattice demonstrations and to the stability record, and a two-name credit cannot capture them. Third, the 1e-18 figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks are recalled by most of us and not checked against primary intercomparisons, so the citation wording should be verified before it is fixed. Finally, if a thorium nuclear clock matures, Ye could be considered again, though I agree with Kroll and Olsson that it is not mature enough to affect this decision.

responses.point: Danielsson is the only member preferring magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B022), arguing that a seven-year gap between the 2011 prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity is the discovery pattern the committee should favour, and that the pairing mechanism being unsettled is a maturity worry but not a disqualifying one.
responses.response: I take his case seriously, and B022 remains my first alternative. The prediction-then-experiment structure is attractive and the phenomenology has been reproduced widely. I still part from him on timing and attribution. After about eight years the nature of the superconducting pairing and the correlated phases is open, and the dependence on twist angle and sample quality is large, so the citation would rest on the existence of the phases and not on an understanding of them. The experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero (Cao, Fatemi, and the Dean, Young and Kim groups) cannot be covered by three names, and I would not want to drop Bistritzer to make room. If we advanced B022 I would name MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. His discovery-versus-capability distinction has some force, but the lattice clock has produced new physics in the form of many-body clock physics and tests of constants, and its confirmation is broader today. I would revisit B022 in a later year if the mechanism is settled.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps the lattice clock first, stresses that the clock accuracy is meaningful only because atomic structure (polarisabilities, blackbody and higher-order light shifts) is understood at the 1e-18 level, and worries that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened and that Lemonde and the ion-clock community are left out.
responses.response: Her point about atomic structure is the best answer to the charge that this is only an instrument prize, because the accuracy rests on control and understanding of systematic shifts to a level where they are physics in themselves. I would use it in the scope statement. I also accept her caution about the redefinition, but I think waiting for it would make the prize depend on a metrological-policy decision and not on the scientific achievement. As to the question I put to her in round 1, her description of Ye's role as pushing accuracy, stability and many-body control makes me more comfortable with the citation wording: the concept to Katori and the demonstrated performance to Ye are two different contributions to one invention. I would word the citation to credit the lattice clock and its development to the 1e-18 level, and let the deliberation record acknowledge Lemonde and the others.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B022 to B025 with some reluctance, noting that this gives priority to maturity over a larger conceptual opening, and that many-body and spin-exchange aspects of the lattice clock are now physics in their own right.
responses.response: I accept the trade-off he describes, and I share his reluctance to some degree. On maturity versus conceptual opening, I would say that B022 may well prove the larger opening, but the committee is not asked to forecast which field will be larger, only to recognise a discovery or invention whose value is already established. His many-body point is useful for the scope statement because it answers the discovery question from inside the physics. Where I differ slightly is the wording of his citation, which adds opening new precision tests of fundamental physics. I would keep the citation shorter, because the tests of constants are still mostly prospective and could overclaim.

responses.point: Eriksson reversed his own opening ranking of the clock (fifth) after weighing attribution and maturity, and says that if the Prize should favour conceptual advances, then tunnelling magnetoresistance (B029) and topological insulators make a stronger claim, while stating the credit risk of Lemonde, Gill, Sterr, Ludlow and Hinkley.
responses.response: I respect that he moved against his own field's candidates. On B029, I agree it deserves a hearing, but his own uncertainty note identifies the problem, since the MgO step is shared with groups and theorists outside the three credited names, so I find the attribution there less clean than for the clock. On the conceptual-advance standard, I would say the magic-wavelength idea is a conceptual advance in how atoms are controlled, not a refinement of the comb or of ion clocks, and that is the distinction I would put in the scope statement. I do not change my alternatives for B029 or B036 on this basis, since I am not a condensed-matter physicist and weigh his judgement of those fields above mine, but the attribution problem is plain from the record.

responses.point: Olsson proposes that the 1e-18 figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks be verified against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed, since several members relied on recalled values, and asks that the deliberation acknowledge the early strontium contributors explicitly.
responses.response: I agree with both requests and would make them conditions of our position. The prize case does not depend on the exact figure, but the citation says near 1e-18, and it should be checked against the published systematic-uncertainty budgets and the intercomparisons before we publish. The citation uses the phrase near 10^-18 for that reason. On the recusal disclosure about Japan, I see no documented collaboration or co-authorship with Katori or Ye, and I would not require recusal, though it should be recorded in the minutes; the same applies to Kroll's stay in Hall's laboratory, which is lineage and not collaboration with the two candidates.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and is an invention that has opened new physics, and not a measurement capability only.
How much weight Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and Hinkley should carry against a two-name credit, which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
The 1e-18 uncertainty figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks are recalled and unverified against primary intercomparisons.
Whether a stricter discovery standard among colleagues would favour B022 despite its unsettled pairing mechanism.
Whether a later thorium nuclear-clock case would involve Ye again.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B025 or B022. I have professional ties to the astroparticle community through PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, so I continue to discount my opening enthusiasm for B007 (IceCube), which is now only my second alternative, and I would consider recusal if it were the leading candidate. I record that I am not an atomic physicist and that I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on the atomic physics of the clock. I see no recusal requirement for the disclosed ties of Olsson (Japan) and Kroll (Hall's laboratory) on B025, since no collaboration with Katori or Ye is documented, and I note that Johansson should stand back from any B016 discussion.
